content: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by injury to the developing brain. It is the most common form of childhood disability, with a global prevalence of 1.5 to 3.8 cases per 1000 live births. Individuals with CP often experience primary impairments such as reduced muscle strength and diminished cardiorespiratory fitness. These impairments lead to difficulties in performing everyday activities, including dressing, walking, and climbing stairs. Exercise is defined as a planned, structured, and repetitive activity aimed at improving physical fitness. It is frequently used as an intervention for individuals with CP. Aerobic and resistance training are thought to improve activity (the ability to perform specific tasks) and participation (engagement in life situations) by addressing the primary impairments associated with CP. However, no comprehensive review of exercise interventions for individuals with CP had been conducted prior to this study. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of exercise interventions on activity, participation, and quality of life in individuals with CP. Secondary outcomes included assessments of body functions and structures. Comparisons were made between exercise interventions and no treatment, usual care, or alternative exercise interventions. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving children, adolescents, and adults with CP. Studies focused on aerobic exercise, resistance training, or mixed training (a combination of aerobic, resistance, and anaerobic training). The search for relevant studies was conducted in June 2016 across multiple databases and trial registries. A total of 29 trials involving 926 participants were included in the review. Most participants were children and adolescents under the age of 19, with a smaller number of studies including young adults (ages 10 to 22) and adults over 20 years old. Males accounted for 53% of the sample. The trials were conducted in various countries, including the USA, Australia, Egypt, Korea, Saudi Arabia, Taiwan, the Netherlands, the UK, Greece, India, Italy, Norway, and South Africa. Of the 29 trials, 26 included participants with spastic CP only, while three included individuals with spastic and other types of CP. Most trials involved participants who could walk with or without assistive devices, while a smaller number included individuals who primarily used wheeled mobility devices. Three trials did not report participants' functional abilities, and only two trials provided information on participants' manual abilities. Eight studies compared aerobic exercise to usual care, 15 compared resistance training to usual care, and four compared mixed training to usual care or no treatment. Two trials directly compared aerobic exercise to resistance training. All trials were judged to have a high risk of bias. The evidence for the effects of exercise interventions was generally of low to very low quality. Aerobic exercise was found to result in small improvements in gross motor function in the short term (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.53) and intermediate term (mean difference [MD] 12.96%). However, aerobic exercise did not improve gait speed in the short term (MD 0.09 m/s) or intermediate term (MD -0.17 m/s). No trials assessed the effects of aerobic exercise on participation or quality of life. Resistance training did not improve gross motor function (SMD 0.12), gait speed (MD 0.03 m/s), participation (SMD 0.34), or parent-reported quality of life (MD 12.70) in the short term. Similarly, resistance training did not improve gait speed (MD -0.03 m/s), gross motor function (SMD 0.13), or participation (MD 0.37) in the intermediate term. Mixed training did not improve gross motor function (SMD 0.02) or gait speed (MD 0.10 m/s) in the short term, but it did result in a small improvement in participation (MD 0.40). There was no significant difference between resistance training and aerobic exercise in terms of their effects on gross motor function in the short term (SMD 0.02). Adverse events were inconsistently reported across the trials. Thirteen trials did not report adverse events, seven reported no adverse events, and nine reported non-serious adverse events. Overall, exercise interventions appeared to be safe for individuals with CP. The authors concluded that the quality of evidence for all outcomes was low to very low, primarily due to small sample sizes and high risk of bias in the included trials. While there is some evidence that aerobic exercise may improve gross motor function in children with CP, it does not appear to improve gait speed. Resistance training does not seem to improve gait speed, gross motor function, participation, or quality of life. Larger, high-quality RCTs are needed to better understand the effectiveness of exercise interventions for individuals with CP. Additionally, research is required to determine whether current exercise guidelines for the general population are appropriate and feasible for individuals with CP.
